Recent work emphasizes aligning item text with collaborative behavior, rather than assuming textual similarity directly predicts the next interaction. [CoCoRec (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.12183) uses fine-grained semantic codes and cross-attention to select relevant textual information; auxiliary masking objectives improve textual–collaborative alignment. [TSSR (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.07623) similarly aligns content and interaction representations through item-level and user-level contrastive objectives. These support selective integration of text, but do not establish effectiveness for a lightweight, scratch-trained GRU encoder. Much recent work depends on pretrained language models: [CLA-Rec (2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10884256/) explicitly extracts LLM description embeddings, then aligns them with collaborative signals, making its implementation unsuitable under the stated constraints.

A constraint-compatible hypothesis, extrapolated from these alignment ideas: tokenize available titles/descriptions, learn small word embeddings from scratch, pool title and description separately, then project and gate their features into item-ID embeddings before the existing GRU. Reuse the same jointly learned item representation for candidate scoring, preserving one network and one checkpoint per category. Begin with mean pooling, bounded text lengths, dropout, and a conservative text gate; compare against the corrected ID-only baseline using macro validation HR@10. Shared tokens could transfer interaction supervision across sparse items, while separate title/description pooling could preserve useful product distinctions. These benefits remain hypotheses requiring validation. Text can encode explicitly stated attributes or entertainment styles; it cannot establish ownership, compatibility requirements, mood, or other unobserved intent.
